finding: The resolve-disposition set and the surviving-set exemption disagree. §8.3 lists three evidenced resolve dispositions as peers — `fixed | wontfix | duplicate` — but §3.4/§4.3 define the *surviving* set as 'findings not resolved wontfix/duplicate' and §3.5 exempts only wontfix/duplicate. That silently treats a `fixed`-resolved finding as still surviving, so a critical/high finding resolved `fixed` keeps its round permanently un-clean under the live recompute of §3.4 — even though `fixed` is the disposition that most strongly signals the defect was addressed. The spec never states this asymmetry or why `fixed` is deliberately excluded from the exemption the other two dispositions get, leaving a reader to reasonably assume all three evidenced resolutions clear a finding from the blocking set.
suggestion: State the intended treatment of `fixed` explicitly in §3.4/§3.5: either (a) exclude `fixed` from the surviving set alongside wontfix/duplicate, or (b) keep the current behavior and add one sentence in §3.5 explaining that a `fixed` finding remains in the surviving set on the round it was recorded (because that round genuinely carried the defect; convergence is achieved by the next fresh round returning nothing), so the disposition list in §8.3 and the exemption set in §3.4/§3.5 are reconciled rather than silently divergent.

finding: The live clean-predicate reads each surviving finding's severity and blocks on `critical`/`high`, but the spec only pins the ABSENT-severity case (§3.4: a round whose findings carry NO per-finding severity is legacy and falls back to the stored clean flag). It never says what a live-recomputed round does with an individual finding whose severity is PRESENT but out-of-vocabulary — an empty string on one row while others are valid, or a reviewer-emitted value like `blocker`/`major` that is not one of `critical|high|medium|low`. Reviewers are LLMs emitting under an informal schema, so this is realistic. A naive `severity in {critical,high}` test silently classifies such a finding as non-blocking and lets a genuinely blocking defect count toward convergence; the implementer must invent whether an unrecognized present severity blocks, is ignored, or is a merge/record error.
suggestion: State the per-finding rule explicitly: either (a) merge/record rejects a finding whose severity is present but not in `critical|high|medium|low` (usage/state error with a hint), or (b) the clean predicate treats an unrecognized present severity conservatively as blocking. Distinguish this from the round-level legacy fallback (which keys on severity being wholly ABSENT), so a mixed round with one bad severity value has defined behavior.

finding: §5.2 asserts an over-specification finding 'does not, by itself, block convergence' and Test 9 (§11.9) asserts 'its presence does not by itself block convergence under blocking'. But §3.2/§4.1 make the blocking decision depend solely on severity (critical/high), while §5.2 states the class only has a 'typical' severity of low/medium and §5.2 confirms the class field is free-form. Nothing forbids a reviewer from stamping an over-specification finding at high severity, in which case it WOULD block a round under 'blocking'. Two engineers write contradictory tests: one uses a low-severity over-spec finding (round clean) and one a high-severity over-spec finding (round not clean) — both faithful to the spec text. Test 9 is not deterministic.
suggestion: State explicitly that convergence-blocking is a function of severity ONLY and the class never affects it; then re-word Test 9 to pin the finding's severity (e.g. 'an over-specification finding at low or medium severity does not block; the same class at high severity blocks, because blocking reads severity not class').

finding: Precedence branch 1 (converged) says next_action names "the phase's forward command (review: decompose / import; audit: proceed)", yet §8.1/§8.2 promise next_action is EXACTLY ONE command string an agent runs verbatim. "decompose / import" is two things, and `decompose` is not a tp subcommand at all (decomposition is agent work; `tp import <file>` is the only tool command). The implementer cannot emit a single concrete command: `tp import` needs a tasks-file argument tp does not know at review-convergence time, and "decompose" has no command form. This is unlike branch 2, which emits a concrete `tp review <file> --resolve[-all] ...` template. The exact string emitted for a converged review round is left to guess.
suggestion: Pin the literal forward-command string for a converged review round (e.g. a fixed hint like `"decompose the spec into tasks, then tp import <tasks.json>"`, or the concrete `tp import` invocation if the target path is derivable), and clarify whether next_action for this branch is a runnable command or a directive — since "decompose" is not a command, the single-command promise needs a stated exception or a rewording.

finding: §8.2 requires next_action to name 'exactly one command', but branch 1 describes the forward action as 'review: decompose / import; audit: proceed'. 'decompose' is not a tp command (there is no `tp decompose`), 'import' is a distinct command, and 'proceed' is not a command at all. So for a converged review round the exact string next_action emits is unpinned (a decompose instruction? `tp import`?), and for a converged audit round 'proceed' names no runnable command. Test 14 (§11.14) asserts a converged round 'names the forward command' without pinning the emitted string, so two engineers assert different literals.
suggestion: Pin the concrete next_action string for each converged case: give the exact command for review convergence (e.g. `tp import <file>`, or a fixed non-command sentinel if decomposition is a manual step) and for audit convergence, and have Test 14 assert that exact string rather than the abstract notion 'forward command'.

finding: §8.4 retains `harness_stale` in the always-on `--compact` path, justified as a 'single short, decision-critical value' on par with `next_action`. But unlike `next_action`, `harness_stale` names no command and never gates (§10.5, §6.4) — it is a diagnostic flag. And the note it refers to, `harness_note`, IS stripped under `--compact` (§8.4), so a compact-mode agent receives `harness_stale: true` with no way to see WHAT framing drifted between rounds and no action the bare boolean licenses. A value that neither gates, nor names the next command, nor can even be acted on in compact (its explanatory note is gone) does not meet the decision-critical bar §8.4 itself sets for surviving compaction — it is exactly the human-facing diagnostic category `--compact` exists to strip.
suggestion: Either strip `harness_stale` under `--compact` alongside `harness_note` (both are wrapper-drift diagnostics, not per-call decision inputs), or state the concrete decision a compact-mode agent makes from `harness_stale` given `harness_note` is unavailable to it.
